title: Vector Representation and Operations

findings.finding: Students must classify sums of vectors before being told that adding vectors produces a vector.
findings.breakdown: The rules permit scalar multiplication and prohibit scalar–vector addition, but do not establish whether vector–vector addition is valid.
findings.checked: No preceding teaching supplies this rule. Geometric vector addition is introduced in the next topic, after these classification tasks.
findings.assumptions: Vector notation is new to these students; no calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p6-interpret-b, insert: “Adding two vectors gives a vector. In 5a+b, where a and b are vectors, 5a is a ___, so adding b gives a ___.” Answers: vector; vector. Retain the booklet’s vector typography.

findings.doneWhen: The vector-addition rule is supplied before students independently classify vector sums.

findings.finding: Connect the constructed sum and difference through cancellation.
findings.breakdown: Adding the two resultants exposes cancellation of b and −b.
findings.checked: The resultants are (3,0) and (1,2); their sum is (4,2)=2a. Addition, negative vectors and scalar multiplication have been taught.
findings.assumptions: Grid displacements use right and up as positive directions.

repair.proposal: Append (d) “Draw the sum of your resultant vectors from parts a and b.” Answer: 4 squares right and 2 squares up. (e) “Explain why this result is twice a.” Answer: b and −b cancel, leaving a+a=2a.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up uses the existing constructions to identify 2a.

findings.finding: The conclusion “The two vectors are not scalar multiples of each other; they are not parallel” relies on an unstated relationship between the named vectors.
findings.breakdown: Unequal coefficient ratios establish nonparallelism only when the two underlying directions are nonparallel. Three named vectors in two dimensions cannot be treated as independent directions.
findings.checked: For a=b≠0, p22-example-right gives 10a and 20a, which are parallel. In p22-h, taking nonparallel a,b and c=−3b gives 2a and 4a. p21-component-j explicitly treats the relationship between different vector letters as unspecified.
findings.assumptions: These are two-dimensional vectors; distinct letters alone do not establish nonparallel directions.

repair.proposal: Before p22-example-block, state: “For comparisons involving combinations of two named vectors here and in Exercise 1, assume those two named vectors are nonparallel.” Replace p22-h with the pair 2a−3b and 4a+6b, using vector typography. Their coefficient multipliers disagree, so they are not parallel under the stated assumption.

findings.doneWhen: The negative conclusions compare coefficients of two explicitly nonparallel directions, including the revised p22-h.

findings.finding: The instruction to find r:s requests a defined ratio that the given vectors cannot produce.
findings.breakdown: The component equations imply s=3r and r=4s, hence r=s=0. The resulting 0:0 is undefined.
findings.checked: Calculated ra+sb=(6r−2s)i+(−r+4s)j. Its only zero is r=s=0. Earlier arithmetic and parallelism teaching cannot yield a defined ratio for these nonparallel vectors.
findings.assumptions: The task requests a ratio rather than asking whether one exists; calculator access is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Keep a=6i−j and change b to −12i+2j. Keep the instruction. Answer: r:s=2:1.

findings.doneWhen: Both component equations yield the same defined ratio from a nonzero cancelling combination.

findings.finding: Vary component signs while holding their magnitudes fixed to expose quadrant adjustments.
findings.breakdown: The reference angle stays fixed while inclination changes.
findings.checked: For (3,4), (−3,4), (−3,−4), (3,−4), inclinations round to 53°, 127°, 233°, 307°. For (−5,2), inclination rounds to 158°. The preceding teaching supplies the reference-angle method; existing practice has no complete fixed-magnitude sign run.
findings.assumptions: Use a scientific calculator in degree mode and column notation.

repair.proposal: After p34-q2-f, add one instruction: “Predict how each sign change affects the direction before calculating.” Append g (3,4), h (−3,4), i (−3,−4), j (3,−4), then unpatterned k (−5,2), all as columns. Answers: 53°, 127°, 233°, 307°, 158°. Only signs vary during g–j.

findings.doneWhen: The run compares all four quadrants using one reference angle, followed by an unpatterned item.

findings.finding: Compare normalisation of vectors with magnitudes greater than, equal to and less than one.
findings.breakdown: The run exposes that normalisation may shorten, preserve or lengthen a vector while preserving its direction.
findings.checked: The proposed vectors have magnitudes 10, 1 and 1/2; each normalises to (3/5)i+(4/5)j. The unpatterned vector normalises to (2i−j)/√5. All required operations are taught by p38.
findings.assumptions: Exact fractional and surd answers are used.

repair.proposal: Append: “Predict which vectors will have the same unit vector.” Add (d) a=6i+8j; (e) a=(3/5)i+(4/5)j; (f) a=(3/10)i+(2/5)j. Answer for each: â=(3/5)i+(4/5)j. Follow with unpatterned (g) a=2i−j; answer: â=(2i−j)/√5. Direction stays fixed during d–f while magnitude varies.

findings.doneWhen: The sequence includes shortening, unchanged length and lengthening, followed by an unpatterned vector.

findings.finding: Four proof tasks in p47-q12 repeat earlier complete identities without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: Parts b, d, e and f reproduce the respective earlier tasks with unchanged endpoints, signs and coefficients.
findings.checked: Compared all four later identities with their worked or guided predecessors. There are no additional givens or diagrams distinguishing them. Asking students to show steps and name laws does not state a specific repetition purpose.
findings.assumptions: The supplied material contains the purposes attached to these tasks.

repair.proposal: Replace later copies, retaining arrows over every endpoint pair: b, prove 2AB−2CB+2CD=2AD; d, prove 3PR−3QR+3QS=3PS; e, prove 2EG−2EF−2GF=4FG; f, prove 3PT−3PR−3TR=6RT. Expected simplified left sides: 2AD, 3PS, 4FG and 6RT respectively. Retain the instruction to show steps and state laws.

findings.doneWhen: Each later copy has changed coefficients and a correct corresponding identity.

findings.finding: The topic lacks review of magnitude calculation and quadrant-based inclination before combining them with point-to-point subtraction.
findings.breakdown: p51-example-content requires recalling both earlier methods while applying the new position-vector formula.
findings.checked: Magnitude and inclination are taught on p31–33. The immediately preceding point-to-point topic and its supplied exercise do not rehearse them. p48–50 rehearses representations and subtraction, but neither missing method.
findings.assumptions: A scientific calculator in degree mode is available. The missing rehearsal concerns formula selection and quadrant decisions, not calculator evaluation.

repair.proposal: Before p48-definition-text, add: (a) Find the exact magnitude of 3i−4j. Answer: 5. (b) Using a sketch, find the inclination of 5i−3j to 1 d.p. Answer: 329.0°. (c) Using a sketch, find the inclination of −3i+j to 1 d.p. Answer: 161.6°. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse magnitude and quadrant decisions before combining them with point-to-point subtraction.

findings.finding: Connect equal consecutive displacements with the complete displacement and its magnitude.
findings.breakdown: The existing parallelism calculation yields equal vectors AB and BC, allowing students to connect addition with doubling.
findings.checked: Parallelism gives k=11, AB=BC=(3,4), AC=(6,8), |AB|=5 and |AC|=10. All required methods are available by the end of the topic.
findings.assumptions: Use the value of k obtained in the existing question.

repair.proposal: Append (b) “Write AC as a column vector.” Answer: (6,8). (c) “Find |AB|.” Answer: 5. (d) “Find |AC|.” Answer: 10. (e) “Explain why AC=2AB for these points.” Answer: AB=BC=(3,4), so AC=AB+BC=2AB. Use arrows over endpoint pairs.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up connects the existing parallelism result with equal displacements and doubled magnitude.

findings.finding: The first guided task combines non-midpoint division, parallelogram side transfers and route selection immediately after a staged midpoint example.
findings.breakdown: Several decisions change together, and the three intermediate prompts used in the example disappear.
findings.checked: p41 supplies parallelogram transfers, but no preceding teaching combines them with non-midpoint division. p56-guided-2 already bridges ratio division through whole-side, divided-side and connecting-vector parts. Its results are BC=4a−3b, BP=(4/3)a−b and AP=(1/3)a+3b.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary ratios and parallelogram properties are prior knowledge.

repair.proposal: Place p56-guided-2 before p56-guided-1, retaining all three parts.

findings.doneWhen: Students practise non-midpoint division in the existing staged structure before the combined parallelogram task.
